narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your undergraduate GPA was actually the strongest positive element in your profile. At 3.70 it sits well above the average of accepted students (3.23), which helped pull the prediction toward passing. However, this advantage was outweighed by two stronger signals that pointed toward failure.

Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the most influential reasons for the rejection. You placed in the bottom decile (1st) after your first year and only slightly higher (2nd decile) by your third year. In contrast, students who were accepted typically ranked around the 6th decile on average. These unusually low rankings pushed the model strongly toward predicting bar exam failure.

Your middle family income, full-time study plans, LSAT score of 28 (well below the accepted average of 37), gender, and race played no role in the decision. The system focused solely on academic performance signals.

To improve your chances, you should consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score and, if possible, strengthen your academic record through additional coursework or a master’s program that demonstrates higher performance in a rigorous environment. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (248 words)
